title: When Humor Hurts: The Trouble with Sarcasm
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. sets out to test whether sarcasm belongs in a teacher's classroom humor, admitting that his stance softened as he researched and that he is himself a sarcastic person. He grounds the concern in teacher credibility and student motivation rather than in students being too sensitive: offending a student damages the beliefs that sustain effort, whether or not the offense was intended. He traces the word's Greek origin of tearing flesh and notes the cultural pull of online mockery, then gives three reasons to be more careful: gentle humor offers the same benefits, sarcasm risks student wellbeing, and practicing contempt shapes the teacher's own heart. A story from his marriage shows how sarcasm is an indirect way of communicating hurt. He ends with an honest caveat about playful banter with a student he respects, and a call for self-examination.
points: Humor's benefits are real, but the same literature warns that sarcasm and ridicule can offend, create tension and damage teacher credibility, which in turn undercuts student motivation.
Self-deprecation and gentle puns deliver the benefits of humor without the risks, and they model joy at no one's expense.
Sarcasm can be a symptom of the teacher's own bitterness, so the impulse to use it is a cue for introspection rather than only a stylistic choice.
Sarcasm communicates indirectly, protecting the speaker while harming the listener, which is why direct (if harder) communication is the better route.
quotes: We know that teacher credibility can be negatively affected, especially by offensive misbehaviors. This loss in credibility affects the motivation of offended students, as credibility is one of the five key beliefs beneath motivation.

As well, when we offend a student with sarcasm — whether the insult is intentional or not! — that student is more likely not to identify with our classroom setting and devalue the work we ask them to do. The five beliefs, in short, are critically damaged when we offend a kid.

When a student who is the object of sarcasm smiles, you really do not know if the student thinks the comment is humorous or is, instead, plotting revenge [or nursing pain]. Besides, there are plenty of sources of good classroom humor without sarcasm.

When I use the occasional bad pun or self-deprecating irony, I don't run those risks. Instead, I'm modeling for my students how to experience joy at the expense of no one, and how to warmly laugh at one's limits and shortcomings.

Instead, I want to use the sarcastic comments that bubble up inside my mind as clues to finding the bitterness and contempt I harbor in my heart. When I find it — towards a decision I don't like, or a politician, or a group of people, or what have you — I want to rid myself of it.

The trouble with this kind of communication, we found, was that it was so indirect. It didn't tell the other person what was going on inside. It protected the self and harmed the other — at the expense of both.

My study of humor in the classroom, and sarcasm specifically, has me ending here: the humor that's most beneficial is wholesome — meaning that it's a humor that all can enjoy. It doesn't hurt or offend or minimize another human being.
